references.text: The prophecy that the suffering servant would die to bear the sins of many, so that the nation would not perish, is a direct parallel to Caiaphas' prophecy that one man should die for the people.
The description of the servant being counted among the transgressors and bearing the sins of many reflects the idea that Jesus' death benefits the entire nation.
The same prophecy is repeated shortly afterward in the same chapter, where John explains that Caiaphas' words were actually a prophecy that Jesus would die for the nation.

The author immediately clarifies after the prophecy that it did not apply only to the Jewish nation, but also to gather God's scattered children, further developing the theme that one death saves many.

The Letter to the Hebrews describes how Jesus became a merciful and faithful high priest to make atonement for the people's sins, a direct fulfillment of the principle that one death saves the nation.
The teaching that Christ was sacrificed once to take away the sins of many corresponds directly with the idea that one person's death prevents the entire nation from perishing.
